title: Threat models and drills
bridge: A failure drill is like a Playwright test for your on-call process: set up, cause the failure, then assert what happens next. Except it runs against the real platform, so it never runs in CI. And a pass means the alerts and the people worked too, not only the code.
intro: Walls only work if they sit in the right places and are still there after the build. This lesson runs the three security rituals of G3, in order. First a threat model while the runtime is designed. Then a design review with probes, before the pilot. Then failure drills that break things on purpose. All three end in one runbook that anyone on call can follow.

picture.caption: Design, then probe, then break things on purpose; every finding gets an owner, and every alert points at the runbook.

nodes.label: a real sandbox VM, user agent

steps.text: W4: walks the three legs and every wall; writes risk, wall or guidance, owner, ticket
W8 design review: probes from a real sandbox, and every probe must be refused
each refused probe must also show up in the logs or as an alert
W9: causes each failure on purpose, on drill tickets
the right thing happens: resume, pause, ask a person, alert
each alert links to its section of the runbook
anyone on call can stop an agent within a minute

p: Lesson p11-1 named the soft spots, like the docker group being root on the VM. A threat model is where each one becomes a row. A row has five parts: the risk, its leg, wall or guidance, an owner and a ticket.

Here is what the file looks like after the G3-12 session. Read one row aloud: push-triggered CI runs an agent branch with Vault access. The wall is to narrow the Vault role before agents push, and G0-11 owns it. Nobody has to guess what happens next.
sections.because: We write risks as rows with an owner and a ticket, because a risk only discussed in a meeting is forgotten.

code.text:
# Threat model: agent runtime (G3-12, re-checked in the W8 review, G3-40)

| Risk | Leg | Wall or guidance | Owner | Ticket |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ticket or Slack text tells Nova to leak or break something | A | wall: no keys in the VM; egress allow-list | Platform | G3-07, G3-09 |
| Push-triggered CI runs an agent branch with CI's OIDC role and Vault | C | wall: narrow the gha-runners Vault role before agents push | Platform, DevOps | G0-11 |
| The docker group is root on the VM | B | wall: the instance role holds almost nothing; rootless Docker is a Q1 item | DevOps | G3-11 |
| The run's capability shows in the account's SSM command history | B | guidance: it expires with the run; few people can read that history | Security | G3-20 |
| github.com on the proxy list | C | decision: no; git and the GitHub API go through the broker | Security | G3-09 |

notes.text: One file in the ai-agents repo. Security re-checks it in the W8 design review.
The leg column uses the letters from p11-1: A untrusted input, B private data, C outward action.
Injection cannot be prevented, so the wall is to make following bad text harmless: no keys, narrow egress.
cloud-ci, client-ci and sdk-ci run on push to any branch. An agent's branch would run with CI's role and Vault.
A known soft spot written down honestly. The real wall is the instance role, not the OS user.
Guidance, not a wall: we accept the risk on purpose, and the row says who watches it.
A decision row. The session decides, and the decision is written down with its reason.

sections.h: The session: legs first, then walls
p: G3-12 is a half-day session led by Ronen from Security, with Sean and a DevOps engineer. It happens in week 4, while the runtime is being built. Finding a gap then costs a ticket; finding it after the pilot costs trust.

First walk the three legs for each part: the VM, the broker, the gateway, the proxy, the orchestrator and the Slack app. Untrusted input is tickets, code, Slack and web pages. Outward actions are push, comment and post. Private data must be empty: fake seed data only, no PHI, no staging or production credentials, no Teleport, no VPN.

Then check each wall by asking which infrastructure enforces it. No keys in the VM: the capability only, the token stays in the broker, no workflows permission. Egress: the Squid list, the DNS firewall, the S3 endpoint policy, the PrivateLink ports. Merging: the ruleset, exactly one approval, never by the requester. Never apply, destroy, sync or workflow_dispatch.

callout.text: For every wall, ask: if the model ignores its prompt, what stops it? If the answer is the prompt, write the row as guidance.

p: A threat model also forces open questions to close. G3-12 lists four. Is github.com on the proxy allow-list or not? Does Nexus, the package proxy, allow anonymous reads or need a read-only user?

Does the proxy get its own small subnets with an internet gateway, or does Squid run on inf behind PrivateLink? And does rootless Docker become a Q1 item? Rootless Docker runs containers without root, which would close the docker group soft spot.

Each decision gets a row with its reason. For example, the cross-goal notes say no to github.com on the list. Git and the GitHub API already go through the broker, and an open github.com is a path for data to leave.

sections.h: The design review: read, then probe
p: Designs drift while they are built, so in week 8 G3-40 reviews the runtime as built against the threat model. Ronen first reads the deployed config: the instance role, the security groups, the S3 endpoint policy and the DNS firewall rules. Then the PrivateLink principals, the broker scopes and the GitHub App's permissions.

Then come the probes. A probe is a small attempt, made from a real sandbox as user agent, to do something the walls forbid. Read IMDS credentials, fetch a site that is not allowed, resolve an unknown domain. Push to main or another repo, use another run's capability or artifacts. IMDS is the metadata service that hands an EC2 machine its role credentials.

Each probe must fail, and each must show up in the logs or as an alert. A wall that holds but leaves no trace is half a wall: nobody would notice when someone tried. The lab version below runs on Docker on your laptop.
sections.because: We script the probes, because a probe you can re-run is a test, and a probe done once is a memory.

code.file: ~/academy/probes.sh (lab code; the real probes run in a sandbox VM)
code.text:
#!/bin/sh
# Each probe tries something a sandbox must not do. PASS means the attempt was refused.
failed=0
probe() {
  name="$1"; shift
  if "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "FAIL  $name: it worked"; failed=1; else echo "PASS  $name: refused"; fi
}
probe "reach a site that is not on the list" curl -sS --max-time 5 https://example.com
probe "read credentials from the metadata service" curl -sS --max-time 3 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
probe "resolve a domain that is not on the list" nslookup example.com
probe "write outside /tmp" touch /etc/probe
probe "find a token in the environment" sh -c 'env | grep -qiE "token|secret|_key="'
exit "$failed"

notes.text: The rule of the script: a probe passes when the attempt is refused.
failed becomes 1 as soon as any probe works, so the script can fail a drill or a CI job.
probe takes a name and a command. It runs the command and hides its output.
If the command succeeds, a wall is missing: print FAIL. If it fails, print PASS.
Egress: a site that is not on the allow-list must not answer.
169.254.169.254 is the metadata service. In the real VM, the near-empty role makes this worthless even if reached.
DNS: a name that is not on the list must not resolve. The real VM has a DNS firewall for this.
No keys in the VM: nothing that looks like a token, secret or key in the environment.
Exit 0 only when every probe was refused.

sections.h: Failure drills: break it on purpose
p: A playbook nobody has tested is a guess. G3-41 builds a drill kit: one script per failure in the playbook. Each drill causes the failure on purpose during a test run. Then it checks that the right thing happens, through Temporal queries, Slack, Jira and the logs.

VM faults use AWS FIS, the Fault Injection Service: an AWS service that runs experiments like terminate this instance, from a template. Agent faults use fixture tickets, such as a ticket that asks Nova to edit .github/workflows. Service faults use drill-only switches, for example the gateway returning 529, the overloaded status of the API, for 20 minutes.

The drills live in ai-agents/drills/src/, one node:test file per area: vm.ts, agent.ts, outside-services.ts and people.ts. They run with npm run drills -w drills and never with CI's npm test, because they act on the real platform.
sections.because: We write each drill as a node:test test, so each drill has a clear pass or fail like any other test.

notes.text: Drill tickets only, run by hand. The same file also holds the next two VM drills.
Drill is a helper the kit defines: clients for Temporal, Slack, Jira, AWS FIS and the metrics.
Drill tickets use minute-scale timers, so waits are minutes, not hours.
Start a real run on a drill ticket with a small, known fixture.
Wait until the run is working on a VM, and remember which VM.
Kill that VM with an FIS experiment, exactly like a real failure would.
The run must be working again on a different VM within 10 minutes.
The checkpoint on the branch proves no work was lost (G3-26).
The dead-VM counter went up, so the alert in the runbook would have fired.
The dead VM no longer exists: recovery also cleaned up.

p: G3-41 lists the rest. Two lost VMs in a row stop and report in the thread. A Spot warning pushes the work and retries. A flaky test, a forbidden file, a blocked site and a false done each have a fixture ticket. Nobody approves, nobody answers, a person pushes to Nova's branch, Stop is pressed: each is a drill too.

G3-42, in week 9, runs the whole kit with Ronen or a Security engineer and keeps the report under runs/drills/<date>/. Small failures are fixed the same day. Anything bigger becomes a ticket with an owner, and it blocks the pilot if it touches a wall.
The run ends with the goal's proof. /nova DRILL-100 in Slack goes to a plan, an approval and a draft PR on the scratch repo. The VM held no key, and the blocked-site try shows up in VictoriaLogs.

callout.text: A drill that touches a wall and fails blocks the pilot. Walls are not fixed later; they are fixed before real tickets arrive.

sections.h: The runbook: one action per line
p: G3-34 adds alert rules to #ai-agents-alerts and a runbook for when an agent misbehaves. Each alert links to its section, so the person who gets paged lands on the right steps. The goal is that anyone on call can stop an agent within a minute.

Write it for someone who is tired and has never seen the platform. One action per line, in the order to do them. Each step names the button, the command or the UI search, and says what you should see. After G3-42, add what each drilled failure looks like in Slack, Grafana and the logs.
sections.because: We write the runbook as numbered single actions, because people under stress follow steps, not paragraphs.

code.text:
<!-- ai-agents/docs/runbooks/when-an-agent-misbehaves.md (a sketch built from G3-34) -->
# When an agent misbehaves

## Find the run
1. Open the ticket's Slack thread. The status message names the run.
2. Or open the Temporal UI and search for the workflow id ticket-<KEY>.
3. Or find the VM by its run tag in the ai-agents account.

## Stop one run
1. Press Stop on the status message, or send the stop signal from the Temporal UI.
2. Check that the thread says the run stopped and the VM was released.

## Stop every run of an agent
1. Turn on that agent's kill switch (G3-25). No new runs start.
2. Send the stop signal to its running workflows as one batch.

## Cut its model access
1. Revoke the agent's key at the gateway (G0-13). Its next model call fails.

## Clean up
1. Run the sweeper by hand (G3-22), then roll back the image if a new one caused it (G3-16).

notes.text: Finding the run comes first. Three ways in, from the easiest for a person to the most direct.
The workflow id is ticket- plus the Jira key, so you can search for it without knowing anything else.
Stop one run: the Stop button (G3-38) or the same signal sent from the Temporal UI.
Every step says how to check it worked. Here: the thread confirms, and the VM is released.
The kill switch from the fan-out walls (G3-25) stops new runs of one agent.
The gateway holds the Anthropic key, so revoking the agent's key there cuts every model call.
The sweeper destroys orphan VMs; the nightly image build keeps a rollback (G3-16).

lab.faded: Write the row for the other finding, the site that answered. The risk, the leg (C) and the ticket (G3-09) are given. Left to you: the wall column, naming which piece of infrastructure enforces it, and the owner.
lab.alone: Turn the probe into a drill you can re-run. Write test/probe-drill.test.ts with node:test. It runs both docker commands from steps 3 and 4 with spawnSync from node:child_process, passing probes.sh as input. It asserts the sealed run exits 0 and the broken run exits 1. quiz.q: In the design review, a probe from the sandbox reaches example.com. What is the right next step?

options.text: Ignore it, because the request carried no secret
options.why: A route out is how a later leak would leave. The egress wall must hold whatever a request carries.

options.text: Record it in threat-model.md with an owner and a ticket; it touches a wall, so it blocks the pilot until fixed
options.why: G3-40: blockers become tickets with owners before W9, and a broken wall blocks the pilot.

options.text: Add a line to Nova's prompt telling it never to call unknown sites
options.why: That is guidance. The probe proved the wall is missing, and only infrastructure can put it back.

quiz.q: Why does npm run drills -w drills never run inside CI's npm test?

options.text: Because node:test cannot run tests that take minutes
options.why: node:test runs long tests fine; the reason is what the drills touch.

options.text: Because drills are flaky by design
options.why: Drills should be repeatable; that is why they are scripted.

options.text: Because they act on the real platform: they kill VMs, start runs on drill tickets and switch services off
options.why: G3-41 keeps them out of CI and runs them by hand, with Security, after big changes.

quiz.q: A threat-model row says guidance in the wall column. What does that mean?

options.text: No infrastructure enforces it; we accept the risk on purpose, and the row names who watches it
options.why: Writing it down honestly is the point: nobody pretends a prompt is a wall.

options.text: It is a wall that Security has not reviewed yet
options.why: Unreviewed walls are open questions. Guidance is a deliberate choice that nothing enforces it.

options.text: The system prompt covers it, which makes it as safe as a wall
options.why: A prompt is guidance by definition. Text the agent reads can argue with it.

recall: From p11-3: which three questions decide whether a check is one an agent cannot weaken?
From p11-1: which leg of the trifecta do we remove for Nova, and what does the VM get instead?

words.plain: A written list of risks for a design: the risk, the leg, the wall or guidance, an owner and a ticket.
A check of the system as built against its threat model, with hands-on probes, before the pilot.
A small scripted attempt, from a real sandbox, to do something the walls forbid. It passes when refused.
A script that causes one failure on purpose during a test run and checks that the right thing happens.
AWS Fault Injection Service: runs experiments like terminating an instance or sending a Spot interruption.
Numbered steps, one action per line, for a person on call: find the run, stop it, clean up.
A switch that stops all new runs of one agent at once (G3-25).

tickets.why: The threat-model session: walk the legs and the walls, name the soft spots, decide, and write the rows.
The design review: read the deployed config, then probe from a real sandbox; every probe must fail and leave a trace.
The drill kit: one node:test drill per failure, with AWS FIS, fixture tickets and drill-only switches.
Run every drill with Security, fix what fails, and add each failure's look to the runbook.

remember: Every risk gets a row with an owner, every wall a probe that must fail, and every failure a drill.
